The interview rehearsal

Sunday, 1 February 2036, evening. Ioana has her naturalisation interview at the Rhône prefecture on Thursday. Julien quizzes her in the kitchen like an official, and Rose-Hélène writes down the answers.
Mrs Popescu, supposing you became French, what would change for you?
I could vote in all elections. And I would no longer feel like a guest in my own country.
That’s good. But what if he asks you the date of the French Revolution?
1789. I know it better than the date of my wedding — your father makes me repeat it every evening.
Next question. Supposing you were asked to give up your Romanian nationality, what would you do?
I would refuse. But France accepts dual nationality, and so does Romania. As long as your file is complete, you can keep both.
And even if they said no, you’d still be Romanian in your head, wouldn’t you?
In my head, in my heart and in my kitchen. No decree can change that.
In the event that the official asked you why you want to be French, what would you say?
That I have two children born in Lyon, a job here, and a neighbour who taught me that you belong to the place where someone answers you.
If nothing else works, you can whistle the three notes. It always works.
(he laughs) Without a minimum of seriousness, you’ll scare the official.
By being myself, I won’t scare anyone. Otherwise, too bad: I’ll come back next year.

“Na-tü-ra-lee-za-syõ”: “u” = “ü”, “s” between vowels = “z”.
“See-twa-yẽ”: “oy” = “wa-y”, nasal “en” = “ẽ”.
“Pray-fek-tür”: “u” = “ü”, final “e” silent.
“Kã-byẽ-mem”: the “d” is not linked, two nasal vowels.
1. À supposer que, en supposant que, en admettant que + subjunctive
These expressions introduce a hypothesis that the speaker is only imagining. They are followed by the SUBJUNCTIVE:
Supposing all goes well, she will be French in June.
Admitting he were right, that changes nothing.
Let’s suppose she refuses. What would happen?
After “si” you never use the subjunctive, but after “à supposer que” you DO: “à supposer qu’il vienne” ✓, “à supposer qu’il viendra” ✗.
2. Pour peu que + subjunctive
“Pour peu que” = “as long as…, if only…”: a minimal condition with a big effect:
As long as your file is complete, you can keep both.
It only takes a little rain for the street to flood.
Simpler synonym: “Il suffit que + subjunctive”: “Il suffit qu’on l’écoute pour qu’elle raconte sa vie.”
3. Si jamais, au cas où, dans l’hypothèse où
indicative (like “si”)
Si jamais il te demande la date, réponds 1789.
Prends ton passeport, au cas où on te le demanderait.
conditional (formal)
Dans l’hypothèse où l’agent vous interrogerait…
Tu peux venir, à condition que tu sois à l’heure.
“Si jamais” ≠ “si… jamais”. “Si jamais tu viens” = if you ever come. “Si tu ne viens jamais” = if you never come.
4. Quand bien même + conditional
“Quand bien même” (even if, formal) expresses a hypothesis that does NOT change the conclusion. It is followed by the CONDITIONAL in both halves:
Even if they said no, you would still be Romanian.
Even if he were right, I wouldn’t change my mind.
In everyday speech: “Même si + indicative”: “Même s’ils disaient non, tu resterais roumaine.”
5. Conditions without “si”
By being myself, I won’t scare anyone. (gerund = if I am)
Without a minimum of seriousness, you’ll scare people. (sans + noun)
Unless you revise everything, you’ll fail. (à moins de + infinitive)
For lack of time, she couldn’t revise. (faute de + noun)
Revise well, otherwise you’ll be back next year. (sinon = otherwise)
These constructions make a text more elegant. In the DELF B2 exam, use at least two to avoid repeating “si”.

Les deux clés

Ioana had submitted her naturalisation file in April 2035, on her return from Bucharest, the day after Sorina said yes in front of the piano. She had been thinking about it for years without ever daring to do it. She had always found a reason to wait: work, the children, papers to translate. But coming back from the Maison Stan, she had understood that she no longer wanted to be a guest anywhere.

The file weighed more than a kilo. It contained her birth certificate translated by a sworn translator, her payslips for the past five years, her tax notices, her employment contract, her two children’s birth certificates, a certificate of her level of French and a two-page cover letter. Julien had reread it eleven times. Amina, whom nobody had asked, had turned it into an eighty-three-line spreadsheet.

The hardest part had been the birth certificate. The original was in Iași, in a drawer of Grandma’s chest, under a pile of embroidered tablecloths. Grandma had refused to post it. Supposing it got lost, she had said, her granddaughter would no longer officially exist, either in Romania or in France. She had insisted that Dan take it to Lyon himself, by train, in an envelope sewn inside his jacket.

Dan had made the journey in two days, with three changes, never taking off his jacket, not even to sleep. In Lyon he had handed the envelope to Ioana with the solemnity of an ambassador. Then he had asked whether he could finally take his jacket off, because it was twenty-eight degrees. Ioana had laughed and cried at the same time. She had said nobody had ever crossed Europe for such a ridiculous piece of paper. Dan had replied that it wasn’t a piece of paper. It was her.

The cover letter had taken the longest. Ioana had written seven versions. The first was too official, the second too sentimental, the third too long. By the fifth she had nearly given up. It was Rose-Hélène who read the sixth over her shoulder and said it sounded like a letter for a competition, not a letter for a country. The seventh version was two pages long. It began with the word “landing”.

Then came the wait. Nine months without news. Ioana checked her letterbox twice a day, then once, then not at all. She ended up believing her file had got lost somewhere between two offices of the prefecture. Julien kept telling her that French bureaucracy was slow but always answered in the end. As long as you’re patient, he said, you get everything. Ioana replied that she wasn’t French — that was precisely the point.

The summons arrived in January 2036, in a brown envelope, on a rainy day. The interview would take place on Thursday 5 February at ten o’clock, at the Rhône prefecture. She had to bring the originals of all documents, an identity document and “sufficient knowledge of French history, culture and society”. Ioana read the sentence three times. She asked Julien what “sufficient” meant. Julien said he had no idea.

So the whole family started revising. Julien asked questions at dinner. Rose-Hélène, who would turn eight in March, had made cards with a question on one side and the answer on the other, like for times tables. Henri-Ion, who had just turned five, couldn’t read the cards, but he already knew the Revolution was in 1789. He shouted it at any moment of the day, even on the bus.

Isabelle taught her the Marseillaise. Ioana already knew it, but only the first verse, and she always went wrong in the same place. In the evenings Isabelle sat at Odile’s piano and they sang together, on the other side of the landing. The neighbours upstairs ended up knocking on the ceiling. The next day they slipped a note under the door: “You sing out of tune, but it’s the right version. Carry on.”

One evening Henri-Ion asked whether he would have to take an exam too, to be French. Julien explained that he had been French since birth, because he was born in France to a French father, and that he was Romanian too, thanks to his mother. Henri-Ion thought for a long time, spoon in the air. Then he declared that he was Franco-Romanian-Lyonnais, and that he wanted a passport for each of the three. Nobody dared tell him the third didn’t exist.

On the Sunday before the interview, Julien held a dress rehearsal in the kitchen. He put on a tie to play the official. Rose-Hélène wrote down the answers in a notebook. Ioana answered everything except one question. When Julien asked her what she would say if the official asked why she wanted to be French, she talked about the landing, about Odile, and about the place where someone answers you. Julien said nothing. He took off his tie.

The night before the interview, Ioana didn’t sleep. She reread her cards until two in the morning, then got up and went out onto the landing, in her pyjamas, barefoot. She sat on the first step of the stairs, where Odile used to sit to water her plants. She stayed there half an hour in the dark. Then, from behind the door opposite, someone whistled three notes, very softly. Isabelle wasn’t asleep either.

On Thursday morning Julien went with her to the prefecture, rue Dunoyer, but he wasn’t allowed in. He waited for her in a café opposite, with a croissant he didn’t eat. In the waiting room there were about twenty people, each with a thick file on their knees. A woman in a hijab revising the French departments. An elderly man holding his wife’s hand. A young Brazilian reciting the Declaration of the Rights of Man under his breath.

Ioana sat down next to the old man. His name was Mr Haddad. He was seventy-nine, had arrived from Syria in 2016 with his wife and grandchildren, and had been waiting for this interview for three years. He asked Ioana where she came from. She said “from Romania”. Then she added “and from the rue d’Austerlitz”. Mr Haddad smiled. He said that he came from Aleppo, and from the rue Paul-Bert, third floor, left-hand door.

The woman in the hijab, sitting on the other side, joined the conversation. Her name was Samira, she was a nurse at the Édouard-Herriot hospital, and she was afraid she didn’t know the departments. Ioana suggested they revise together. For ten minutes they quizzed each other in low voices: Rhône, sixty-nine; Loire, forty-two; Isère, thirty-eight. Mr Haddad listened with a smile. He said that in Aleppo his pupils used to revise like that, in the corridor, the day before exams.

They talked for forty minutes while waiting their turn. About the war, a little. About the children, a lot. About French bread, which he found too soft, and Syrian bread, which he couldn’t find anywhere. He told her he had been a music teacher in Aleppo for thirty years, and that he hadn’t played the oud since arriving in France. His oud had stayed there, in the flat, with everything else. He didn’t know whether the flat still existed.

Then a voice called: “Mrs Popescu?” Ioana stood up. Mr Haddad wished her good luck, in Arabic, then in French. The official waiting for her in a small office was a woman of about fifty, with short grey hair and red glasses. Her name was Mrs Benali. She asked Ioana to sit down, opened the file, and looked at the cover letter for a long time without saying anything.

The first questions were the ones Ioana had revised. The date of the Revolution: 1789. The motto of the Republic: liberty, equality, fraternity. The principle of secularism: the State favours no religion and guarantees everyone’s freedom to believe or not to believe. The name of the river that runs through Lyon with the Rhône: the Saône. Ioana answered quickly, too quickly, like a pupil afraid of forgetting if she slows down.

Mrs Benali put down her pen. She said there was no need to recite. That she wasn’t there to check whether Ioana had learnt a textbook by heart, but to find out who she was. Then she asked a question Ioana hadn’t prepared. Supposing France and Romania one day played each other in a World Cup final, who would Ioana support? Ioana stared at her, speechless. Mrs Benali was smiling behind her red glasses.

Ioana thought about it. Then she answered honestly. She said that even if Romania had a chance of winning, which was unlikely, she would support both. She would cheer for France when France scored, for Romania when Romania scored, and at the end she would be happy whatever happened, because one of her two countries would have won. Mrs Benali burst out laughing. She said it was the best answer she had heard in years.

She added that her own grandfather had arrived from Algeria in 1962, in Vénissieux, to work in a lorry factory. All his life he had supported Algeria and France at the same time, and had spent every match between them cheering for everyone, to his neighbours’ despair. He used to say a man had the right to have two teams, just as he had the right to have two children. You don’t choose between your children.

Then came the question Ioana had been waiting for. Mrs Benali simply asked her why she wanted to become French. Ioana opened her mouth to recite the answer she had prepared. Then she closed it again. She talked about something else. She talked about an old lady who whistled off-key on the other side of a landing, and a young Romanian woman who had had the courage to answer her one evening in 2026, because she felt alone in a country that wasn’t hers.

She said that on that evening, without knowing it, she had become a little French. Not because she had learnt the date of the Revolution, but because someone in this country had waited for her. The rest, she said, was just paper. But she wanted that paper all the same. For her children, born here. To vote. And to be able to say, the next time someone asked whether she was from here, that yes, she was from here too.

Mrs Benali wrote nothing for a long moment. Then she took off her red glasses and wiped them. She said she had seen the film “Répondre” at the cinema with her daughter in January. That she had recognised the name Popescu in the file but hadn’t been sure. That she wasn’t allowed to say what she would write in her report. But that in Ioana’s place she wouldn’t worry too much.

Coming out of the office, Ioana passed Mr Haddad, who was going in. He asked how it had gone. She told him not to recite. To talk about himself. About the rue Paul-Bert, the third floor, the left-hand door. About the oud. Mr Haddad nodded. He went in. Ioana waited for him in the waiting room, though nothing obliged her to. He came out forty minutes later, his eyes red, smiling.

Meanwhile Julien had told the whole story to the waiter, who had told the owner, who had told two customers leaning on the counter. When Ioana walked in, the whole café turned towards her, as if she were coming back from a final. The owner asked whether it had gone well. Ioana said she didn’t know yet. The owner said that, in case of doubt, the coffee was on the house. The two customers applauded anyway, just in case.

In the café opposite, Julien had ordered four coffees while waiting, and had drunk them all. He was shaking more than Ioana. She told him everything: the World Cup, the grandfather from Vénissieux, the red glasses, Mr Haddad. Julien asked whether she thought she had passed. Ioana said she had no idea. But supposing she had failed, at least she would have met a man who played the oud. That was no small thing.

That same evening Ioana wrote to Mariama to tell her about Mr Haddad. Mariama replied an hour later from Dakar. She knew someone in Mirecourt who could make any instrument, even ones he had never seen. The next day Ioana called Gérard Thiébaut. He had never made an oud in his life. He said that would make it all the more interesting. He asked for photos, measurements, and Mr Haddad’s address.

The following Sunday, Mr Haddad invited the whole family to lunch, in a small flat in Vénissieux, on the ninth floor, with a view over the whole city. His wife, Salma, had made a meal for twenty: tabbouleh, hummus, stuffed vine leaves that looked strangely like sarmale. Ioana pointed it out. Salma laughed. She said that if you looked a little closer, all the grandmothers in the world cooked the same thing under different names.

Meanwhile, at school, Mr Bernard had given the whole Year 4 class a presentation to prepare: “Where I come from”. Each child had to bring a map, a photo and an object. Rose-Hélène spent three evenings on her presentation. She drew an enormous map, with Lyon, Bucharest, Iași, Corsica, Dakar and Brest, linked by arrows of every colour. In the centre of the map, in place of Lyon, she drew a landing with two doors.

The presentations lasted a week. Lucas talked about Corsica and the half-green lime tree. A little girl, Yasmine, talked about her grandmother’s Morocco, with a silver teapot. A boy, Tiago, brought a Portuguese football shirt. Another, Malik, said he came from Vaulx-en-Velin, and that was all, and everyone applauded anyway. Mr Bernard said you could perfectly well come from just one place. It didn’t make people any less interesting.

When Rose-Hélène’s turn came, she unfolded her map on the board. She explained that her mother came from Romania, her father from Lyon, and the waltz from Dakar. A classmate asked whether she was French or Romanian. Rose-Hélène thought about it. Then she said she was from the landing. The whole class laughed, except Mr Bernard, who asked what that meant. Rose-Hélène took her harmonica and played three notes.

In the class, several children answered by whistling. They all knew the waltz now. Rose-Hélène said that was what being from the landing meant: coming from anywhere, but knowing there is someone on the other side who will answer. Mr Bernard wrote something in his notebook. That evening he sent Julien a message. He said he had been teaching for twenty-three years and had never heard a better definition of identity.

One Saturday Inès came to babysit. She was in her first year of law, and Rose-Hélène asked her what nationality actually was. Inès took a sheet of paper and drew two columns: rights on one side, duties on the other. Voting, being elected, being protected abroad. Obeying the law, paying taxes, serving on a jury if your name is drawn. Rose-Hélène looked at the two columns. She asked where the column for answering the neighbours was.

On Tuesday 10 March, an official envelope arrived at the rue d’Austerlitz. It wasn’t the decree yet. It was a letter from the prefecture announcing that Mrs Ioana Popescu’s application had received a favourable opinion, and that her naturalisation would be published in the Official Journal in the following weeks. Ioana read the letter standing in the hall, her coat still on, her bag still on her shoulder. Then she sat down on the floor.

Rose-Hélène found her there when she came home from school, sitting on the floor in the hall, the letter in her hand. She thought it was bad news. Ioana handed her the letter. Rose-Hélène read it slowly, following the lines with her finger. When she reached the word “favourable”, she stopped. She asked whether it meant yes. Ioana said it did. Then Rose-Hélène ran to the door opposite and knocked four times.

That same evening Ioana called Iași. She wanted to tell Grandma before anyone else. Grandma listened without a word. Then there was a long silence, longer than eight bars. Ioana thought the line had been cut. At last Grandma’s voice came back, fainter than usual. She asked just one thing: whether her granddaughter, now that she was French, was going to forget Romanian.

Ioana answered in Romanian, at length. She said you don’t forget a language because you learn another. You don’t leave a house because you open a second one. She still dreamt in Romanian, still counted in Romanian, and still swore in Romanian when she stubbed her toe on the table. Grandma laughed. She said she was reassured, especially about the swearing. Then she reminded her that she would turn ninety on Saturday 21 March.

All week Elena called every evening to talk about the menu. There would be ciorbă, sarmale, cozonac, cheese plăcinte and a three-tier cake ordered from the best pastry cook in the neighbourhood. Julien asked how many people were invited. Elena said sixty. Julien asked whether sixty people could really eat all that. Elena replied that in Moldavia you always cook for twice as many, in case someone turns up without warning.

They left for Iași on Thursday 19 March, all four of them, with Isabelle, who had never seen Moldavia. Rose-Hélène had turned eight two weeks earlier. For her birthday present she had asked to go and see Grandma, and nothing else. Henri-Ion had brought Grandma a drawing: a cake with ninety candles, which he had drawn one by one, tongue sticking out, over a whole afternoon.

Grandma still lived in the same small flat, on the fourth floor of a grey block in the Tătărași district, with her plants, her embroidered tablecloths and her old radio. She was waiting for them on the landing, leaning against the door, in her best dress, the blue one from Henri-Ion’s christening. She had refused to let anyone fetch her from the station. She wanted to be at home, on her landing, when they arrived.

When they reached the top of the stairs, out of breath, Grandma didn’t say hello. She whistled three notes. Off-key, of course, more off-key than ever. Rose-Hélène answered on the harmonica before she had even put down her suitcase. Then Grandma took Ioana in her arms for a very long time without a word. Isabelle, watching from the last step, said later that she had felt she was seeing her mother, on another landing, in another language.

On Friday Grandma took them to Copou park, above the city. She wanted to show them a tree. It was a very old lime tree, propped up with iron bars and surrounded by a little railing. Grandma explained that the great poet Mihai Eminescu used to come and write under this tree more than a hundred and fifty years ago, and that all the lovers of Iași still met there. Rose-Hélène put her hand through the railing and touched the bark.

The party took place on Saturday, in a hall rented on the ground floor of the block, because the flat was too small for sixty people. There were the neighbours, the cousins, Grandma’s former colleagues from the textile factory, the local priest, and Elena, who had been cooking for three days. Sorina and Andrei had driven from Bucharest. They had brought a surprise: a video of Viorica, aged ninety-five, wishing her junior a happy birthday.

In the video, Viorica was sitting at the Maison Stan piano. She said that at ninety you were still a young girl, and that you must never let yourself be impressed by numbers. Then she played three notes with one finger. Grandma, who had never met Viorica, answered by whistling at the screen. She said she liked this lady, and that if she ever went to Bucharest she would go and teach her to play with two fingers.

When the cake came, Grandma asked for silence. She had prepared a speech. She had written it on a sheet of exercise paper in blue ink, and she read it with her glasses on the end of her nose. She spoke of her husband, who had died twenty years before. Of the factory, the queues outside empty shops, the winter of 1989. Of her daughter Elena, her grandchildren, her great-grandson who bore a Romanian name and a French name at once.

Then she turned to Ioana. She said she had been afraid on the day her granddaughter left for France, ten years earlier. Afraid of losing her. Afraid she would become a stranger. She had been wrong. Ioana hadn’t become a stranger. She had become someone with two homes. And even if Grandma were no longer there one day, which would happen eventually, she added, Ioana would always have a home in Iași.

She took from the pocket of her dress an old iron key, as long as a finger, tied to a red ribbon. It was the key to her childhood home in the country, in a village near Iași, where she had been born in 1946. The house had been empty for a long time, but it was still standing. Grandma put the key in Ioana’s hand. She said: “You now have two nationalities. You need two keys as well.”

Rose-Hélène looked at the key with great interest. She already had three herself: the one to Odile’s flat, on a blue ribbon, the one to the museum display case, which Mrs Lacroix had never asked for back, and the one to the Corsican wash-house, which Antoine had left her. She asked Grandma whether you could have as many homes as you had keys. Grandma said yes. As long as someone was waiting for you there.

In the evening, after the cake, a cousin brought out an accordion. The whole hall got up to dance the hora, holding each other by the shoulders, in a circle. Grandma, despite her ninety years and her cane, danced two whole rounds. Julien tried to keep up and got his feet wrong at every step, which greatly amused the former colleagues from the factory. Isabelle learnt it in three minutes. She said it was exactly like a waltz, but in a ring.

The next day, Sunday, they all went to see the village house. It was forty minutes from Iași, at the end of a dirt track lined with walnut trees. The house was small and white, with a rusty tin roof and a wooden veranda painted blue. The garden had been overrun by weeds. But in front of the door there was an old lime tree, enormous, just beginning to bud. Rose-Hélène stopped dead when she saw it.

Grandma said this lime tree had been planted by her own father in 1946, on the day she was born. So it was exactly her age. Ninety. Rose-Hélène put her hand on the bark, as she did with the La Duchère lime tree and the Corsican one. She closed her eyes. She said it was alive. Grandma asked how she knew. Rose-Hélène said she didn’t know how. She just knew.

Ioana opened the door with the red-ribboned key. The lock resisted, then gave way with the creak of an old door that hadn’t been opened for years. Inside it was cold and dark. There was a tiled stove, a table, two chairs, and on the wall a yellowed photo of a couple in traditional dress. Grandma said they were her parents, on their wedding day in 1938. She hadn’t seen that photo for thirty years.

They stayed all afternoon. Julien and Dan pulled up the weeds. Isabelle opened all the windows. Henri-Ion found a cat living under the veranda that refused to leave. Ioana sat on the steps with Grandma in the March sun. They hardly spoke. Grandma only asked whether, supposing the house were repaired one day, Ioana would come and spend her summers there. Ioana said yes. With the children. And with the lime tree.

Before leaving, Rose-Hélène did something nobody had asked her to do. She took out of her bag a little bottle of water she had filled at the La Duchère fountain before leaving, as she did for every lime tree she met. She poured the water at the foot of the tree. Then she whistled three notes. Nobody answered. The village was empty, silent. But in the lime tree, a bird nobody could see sang something. That was enough.

Back in Lyon, a small parcel was waiting for Mr Haddad at his local post office. It came from Mirecourt. Gérard Thiébaut had worked on the oud for six weeks, from the photos, the measurements and three long phone calls with a musician from Aleppo who had taken refuge in Marseille. It wasn’t Mr Haddad’s oud. He knew that. But in the box he had slipped a note: “It isn’t as old as yours. It only asks to become so.”

At the Thursday orchestra, the news of the favourable letter had gone round the music stands in a single evening. Amina, seven months pregnant, had added a line to her spreadsheet for the year: “Ioana becomes French”. Bernard Delorme had offered to play the Marseillaise on the trumpet during the ceremony, which the prefecture had obviously not accepted. So the orchestra played the Marseillaise the following Thursday, then the Romanian anthem, then the waltz, and Ioana cried through all three.

The ceremony welcoming new French citizens took place on Friday 24 April 2036 at the Rhône prefecture, in a large drawing room with gilded ceilings. There were sixty-two new French citizens from twenty-seven countries. Each was allowed to invite two people. Ioana had invited Julien and Isabelle. Rose-Hélène and Henri-Ion hadn’t been invited, but they were there anyway, because Isabelle had spoken to the usher at the door, and the usher had seen the film.

The prefect gave a speech about the values of the Republic. Then the new citizens were called one by one to receive their decree and a booklet. When “Mrs Ioana Popescu” was called, Ioana stood up on trembling legs. She shook the prefect’s hand. She took her decree. Walking back to her seat, she saw, in the second row, Mrs Benali in her red glasses, who had no official reason to be there, applauding her.

Mr Haddad was called right after her. He had brought the Mirecourt oud in its case, not knowing whether he would be allowed to open it. At the end of the ceremony everyone stood up to sing the Marseillaise. Sixty-two different accents, one single song, mostly off-key. Ioana went wrong in the usual place. So did Isabelle, out of solidarity. Then, when the singing ended, there was a moment of silence in the great gilded room.

It was Mr Haddad who broke the silence. He opened the case, took out the oud and played three notes. Nobody had given him permission. The prefect frowned, then recognised the tune, like everyone else. On the other side of the room, a small voice answered with a harmonica. Then another voice, whistling. Then another. A woman from Vietnam. A man from Chile. A student from Cameroon. The prefect himself.

After the ceremony nobody wanted to leave. On the steps of the prefecture, in the April sun, Mr Haddad played the oud for half an hour for the sixty-two new French citizens and their families. Samira danced with her children. Mrs Benali stayed to the very end, pretending to wait for someone. Before leaving, she told Ioana that in her job you saw a lot of files go by and forgot most of the faces. She wouldn’t forget this one.

That evening Ioana pinned her decree on the kitchen wall, next to Rose-Hélène’s drawing, the one with the landing at the centre of the world. She hung the red-ribboned key on a nail just below it, next to the flat keys. Then she called Iași. Grandma asked whether it was done. Ioana said yes, she was French. Grandma said: “Good. Now say something in Romanian, so I can check.” Ioana said: “Te iubesc, bunico.” Grandma said that was fine. She hadn’t forgotten anything.

Reading: Testimonies — having two countries
A Lyon magazine published three testimonies about identity from people you know. Notice the hypotheses. Listen to the text twice, then read it aloud. At the end, answer 4 questions.
Témoignages : avoir deux pays

Mariama, 67, retired primary teacher: “I arrived in Lyon in 1994. Supposing someone asked me today where I come from, I wouldn’t know what to answer. From Dakar, of course. But also from Villeurbanne, from my classroom, from my pupils.”

“For thirty years I thought I was from here without being entirely so. Then I went back to Dakar and understood that there too I was no longer entirely from there. Even if I wanted to, I could no longer choose. So I stopped choosing.”

Ioana, architect: “I’m Romanian and I’ve just become French. People often ask me whether I feel more one than the other. Just give me a sarma to taste and I’m Romanian. Just talk to me about bread and I’m from Lyon.”
“My children don’t ask themselves the question. They speak both languages, eat both cuisines, and if anyone ever asks them where they’re from, they answer: ‘from the landing’. I think they’re right.”

Lamine, 41, kora player: “I’m a griot. Where I come from, we say you belong to those whose memory you keep. For lack of papers, I couldn’t stay in France more than a month. But playing the waltz, I feel I have cousins everywhere.”

“If I were given one more passport, I wouldn’t change anything. You don’t need a stamp to know where you’re at home. It’s enough that someone answers when you whistle. Otherwise you’re a stranger everywhere.”
